# On National Wear Red Day, women share the heart symptoms they almost ignored

**By [Your Name]**  
**Health News Feature**

When **Maria Thompson** put on a red sweater Friday morning in **Charlotte, North Carolina**, she said it felt less like a fashion choice and more like a warning sign she wished she had recognized years earlier.

“I thought heart attacks looked like what you see in the movies — someone clutching their chest and falling down,” Thompson said. “Mine felt like pressure, nausea and a strange ache in my jaw. I kept telling myself I was just tired.”

Thompson, 52, is one of many women marking **National Wear Red Day**, the annual awareness day held on the first Friday in February to spotlight heart disease in women. The campaign is part of the broader **American Heart Association’s Go Red for Women** movement, which encourages people to wear red, learn their risk factors and talk with health care providers about prevention.

Heart disease remains the **leading cause of death for women in the United States**, according to federal health officials. Yet doctors and advocates say many women still underestimate their risk — and may miss symptoms that don’t match the classic image of a heart attack.

## ‘I was 39. I didn’t think it could be my heart.’

In **Phoenix, Arizona**, **Tanya Morales**, a mother of two, said she ignored weeks of unusual fatigue before she landed in the emergency room.

“I was 39,” Morales said. “I worked full time, I had kids, I was always exhausted. So when I started feeling short of breath walking up the stairs, I blamed stress.”

Then came the pain between her shoulder blades.

“It wasn’t crushing chest pain,” she said. “It was this deep, uncomfortable pressure. I remember thinking, ‘This is weird,’ but I still didn’t want to make a big deal out of it.”

Doctors later told Morales she had a significant blockage and needed a stent.

Her message on National Wear Red Day is simple: “Don’t wait until you collapse. If something feels wrong, get checked.”

## A campaign built around visibility

National Wear Red Day asks people to wear red clothing or accessories and share photos and stories to raise awareness about women’s heart health. In communities across the country, hospitals, schools, workplaces and local health departments often host blood pressure screenings, educational events and fundraisers.

The **Go Red for Women** campaign emphasizes several key prevention steps: knowing your blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar numbers; not smoking; staying physically active; eating a heart-healthy diet; managing stress; and discussing family history with a clinician.

Advocates also use the day to highlight disparities. Black women, for example, are disproportionately affected by high blood pressure and heart disease, and barriers to care can delay diagnosis and treatment.

## ‘My symptoms were dismissed as anxiety’

For **Denise Walker** of **Detroit, Michigan**, the road to diagnosis was frustrating.

“I went to urgent care twice,” Walker said. “I was told it was probably anxiety or indigestion. But I knew my body. I knew something wasn’t right.”

Walker, 58, said her symptoms included sweating, dizziness and a burning sensation in her chest that came and went. After a third visit — this time to an emergency department — testing showed she had suffered a heart attack.

“I’m not angry at one person,” she said. “But I do think women have to be taken seriously when they say, ‘This feels different.’”

Health experts say women can experience chest pain during a heart attack, but they may also report symptoms such as shortness of breath, nausea, vomiting, back or jaw pain, lightheadedness, extreme fatigue or discomfort in the arms, neck or upper abdomen.

## Survivors turn awareness into action

In **Brooklyn, New York**, **Aisha Reynolds**, 46, now organizes a small Wear Red Day walk with friends and neighbors.

“It started with five of us wearing red lipstick and taking a picture,” Reynolds said. “Now we meet, walk, check in on each other and remind people to schedule their appointments.”

Reynolds was diagnosed with heart failure after months of swelling in her legs and difficulty sleeping flat.

“I thought I was out of shape,” she said. “I didn’t know fluid buildup could be connected to your heart.”

She said National Wear Red Day helps start conversations that might otherwise feel uncomfortable.

“People ask, ‘Why are you wearing red?’ and that opens the door,” Reynolds said. “You can say, ‘Because women are dying from heart disease, and we need to know the signs.’”

## What women should know

Doctors urge anyone with possible heart attack symptoms to call emergency services immediately. They also recommend that women discuss personal risk factors with a health care provider, especially if they have high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, a history of smoking, pregnancy-related complications, autoimmune disease or a family history of early heart disease.

For Thompson, the red sweater is now part of a yearly ritual. She wears it to work, posts a photo online and shares the symptom she once explained away: jaw pain.

“If my story makes one woman stop and call 911 instead of lying down and hoping it passes, then it’s worth telling,” she said.

On National Wear Red Day, survivors say the color is more than a symbol. It is a reminder to listen, ask questions and act early.

“Red gets people’s attention,” Morales said. “That’s the point. Heart disease needs our attention — before it becomes an emergency.”

## NHLBI Campaign Puts Women’s Heart Health in the Spotlight: “Heart Disease Doesn’t Care What You Wear”

Heart disease does not discriminate by age, background, profession—or wardrobe. That is the message behind the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute’s campaign, **“Heart Disease Doesn’t Care What You Wear,”** a public awareness effort designed to remind women that heart disease remains a leading threat to their health, even when it may not look the way many expect.

The campaign, part of NHLBI’s broader work to improve cardiovascular health, uses the familiar symbol of red clothing—especially the red dress—to draw attention to a sobering reality: **heart disease is the leading cause of death for women in the United States.** Yet many women continue to underestimate their personal risk, sometimes dismissing symptoms or delaying preventive care while juggling family, work, and community responsibilities.

Health experts say that gap in awareness can have serious consequences.

“Women often know they should be taking care of everyone else, but they may not recognize when their own risk is rising,” the campaign’s message suggests. “Heart disease can affect anyone, and prevention starts with knowing your numbers, knowing your family history, and taking action early.”

### Family History Can Be a Warning Sign

One of the campaign’s central themes is the importance of understanding **family risk**. A parent, sibling, or close relative with heart disease—especially at a younger age—can increase a woman’s chances of developing cardiovascular problems herself.

But family history is not destiny. Doctors emphasize that knowing this information can help women and their health care providers take preventive steps sooner. That may include more frequent blood pressure checks, cholesterol screening, blood sugar testing, and conversations about weight, pregnancy-related complications, smoking, stress, and other factors that influence heart health.

For many families, the campaign also encourages a broader conversation: What conditions run in the family? Who has had a heart attack, stroke, high blood pressure, diabetes, or high cholesterol? At what age were they diagnosed?

These questions can be lifesaving.

### Lifestyle Changes That Make a Difference

While some risk factors cannot be changed, many can be addressed through everyday choices. NHLBI’s campaign highlights practical steps women can take to protect their hearts, including:

- **Getting regular physical activity**, such as brisk walking, dancing, cycling, swimming, or other movement that fits into daily life  
- **Choosing heart-healthy foods**, including fruits, vegetables, whole grains, lean proteins, and foods lower in saturated fat, sodium, and added sugars  
- **Maintaining a healthy blood pressure and cholesterol level**  
- **Quitting smoking** and avoiding secondhand smoke  
- **Managing stress** and getting enough quality sleep  
- **Keeping medical appointments** and discussing symptoms promptly with a clinician  

The campaign’s message is not that women must make perfect choices. Rather, it encourages sustainable changes—small steps that can build into lasting habits.

Even modest improvements can matter. A daily walk, replacing sugary drinks with water, preparing more meals at home, or taking medication as prescribed can help reduce risk over time.

### Recognizing Symptoms in Women

Another major challenge is that heart disease symptoms in women may be misunderstood or overlooked. While chest pain or pressure is common, women may also experience symptoms such as shortness of breath, nausea, lightheadedness, fatigue, pain in the back, neck, jaw, or arms, or discomfort that does not feel like the “classic” heart attack signs often portrayed in movies.

Campaign advocates urge women not to ignore unusual symptoms—especially if they are severe, sudden, or accompanied by weakness, sweating, or trouble breathing. In an emergency, calling 911 quickly can save heart muscle and save lives.

### Red Clothing as a Public Call to Action

The campaign’s visual centerpiece is red clothing, a bold and accessible symbol of women’s heart health awareness. Across the country, workplaces, schools, hospitals, community centers, and public health organizations host **red clothing awareness events**, inviting participants to wear red to spark conversations about prevention and risk.

These events often include blood pressure screenings, educational booths, fitness activities, panel discussions, social media campaigns, and memorial tributes to women affected by heart disease. The color red serves as both a warning and a rallying cry: pay attention, get checked, and support the women in your life.

Annual red-themed observances, including February events tied to American Heart Month, have helped bring visibility to a disease that was once widely framed as a men’s health issue. By encouraging women and families to wear red, organizers hope to turn awareness into action.

### A Campaign With a Personal Message

At its core, **“Heart Disease Doesn’t Care What You Wear”** is not just a slogan. It is a reminder that heart disease can affect women who appear healthy, women with busy lives, women with no obvious symptoms, and women who may not realize their family history puts them at higher risk.

The campaign asks women to take their heart health personally—and asks families, employers, clinicians, and communities to help make prevention easier.

Wearing red may start the conversation. But the larger goal is clear: more women knowing their risk, making heart-healthy changes, and getting the care they need before a crisis occurs.
